golden_3.title: You want a piece of Pi?

golden_4.title: WE HAVE TO GO BACK!
golden_4.description: Discover the sequence from the Lost series.

golden_8.title: Permission to enter the vacuum granted.

golden_9.title: Engage warp speed!
golden_9.description: Discover the speed of light constant.

legendary_Primer.title: Legendary twins
legendary_Primer.description: Make Primer legendary with twin primes of at least 4 digits (the score and the score + 2).

legendary_Split.title: Divide and conquer
legendary_Split.description: Make Split legendary with a multiple of 2520, divisible by every digit from 1 to 9.

legendary_Boost.title: Square and cube at once
legendary_Boost.description: Make Boost legendary with a sixth power (64, 729, 4096...).

legendary_Digit.title: Mirror, mirror on the wall
legendary_Digit.description: Make Digit legendary with a narcissistic number, equal to the sum of its digits each raised to the number of digits (153 = 1³ + 5³ + 3³).

legendary_Reduce.title: All in binary
legendary_Reduce.description: Make Reduce legendary with a power of 2 of at least 1024.

legendary_Align.title: Perfectly aligned
legendary_Align.description: Make Align legendary with a palindrome that has as many digits as the button's value.

legendary_Fiber.title: The sacred spiral
legendary_Fiber.description: Make Fiber legendary with a Fibonacci number that is also prime (13, 89, 233...).

legendary_Factor.title: Factorially yours
legendary_Factor.description: Make Factor legendary with a score that is exactly a factorial, from 4! = 24.

legendary_Cipher.title: Easy as 1, 2, 3
legendary_Cipher.description: Make Cipher legendary with at least 4 digits in a row, in ascending order (1234, 45678...).

legendary_Plus.title: Powers of ten
legendary_Plus.description: Make Plus legendary with a power of 10, from 100.

legendary_Minus.title: Broken record
legendary_Minus.description: Make Minus legendary with a score made only of the digit of its value, at least 3 digits long (777 for Minus 7).

legendary_Double.title: And then zeros
legendary_Double.description: Make Double legendary with its value followed by zeros, at least 3 digits long (500 for Double 5).

legendary_Half.title: A thousand times
legendary_Half.description: Make Half legendary with a multiple of 1000.

legendary_Mirror.title: Through the looking-glass
legendary_Mirror.description: Make Mirror legendary with a multiple of its mirror that is not a palindrome (8712 = 4 × 2178).

goodwin.name: Goodwin
goodwin.story: A doctor, he was certain he had proved that π equals 3.2. In 1897, he offered Indiana to make it law, and generously gave his discovery to the state’s schools. The House voted yes, unanimously. A math professor happened to be visiting the State House: the Senate postponed the vote. Indefinitely.
goodwin.jab: {clicks}. Indiana’s lawmakers would find you brilliant.

hanyecz.name: Hanyecz
hanyecz.story: On May 22, 2010, he paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas. It was the first known purchase made with bitcoin, and probably the most expensive pizzas in history. He says he regrets nothing.

airy.name: Airy
airy.story: Astronomer Royal. In 1842, the government asked him whether Babbage’s calculating machine could be of any use. Answer: none. The funding was cut, and the computer would wait a century. A few years later, he would also be blamed for letting the discovery of Neptune slip away. A consistent man.
airy.jab: The machine’s report on your usefulness: about that of a horoscope.

preece.name: Preece
preece.story: An engineer at the British Post Office. In 1879, he told a parliamentary committee that the telephone was fine for Americans: the British had plenty of messenger boys. He was knighted anyway.
preece.jab: You would make an excellent messenger: fast, obedient, no questions asked.

stoll.name: Stoll
stoll.story: In 1986, he went after a hacker who was selling the KGB secrets stolen from his laboratory’s computers. In 1995, he mocked in Newsweek those who believed we would one day buy books on the Internet. Today, he sells Klein bottles. Online.
stoll.jab: Admit it: you bought the solution online.

stifel.name: Stifel
stifel.story: Mathematician and pastor. His calculations set the end of the world for October 19, 1533, at 8 a.m. His parishioners left everything to wait for it with him. At 8:01, the mood changed. He made up for it later: he is the one who coined the word “exponent”.
stifel.jab: The machine expected the end of the world before your success. It is almost disappointed.

brahe.name: Brahe
brahe.story: At 20, he lost a piece of his nose in a duel over who was the better mathematician, and wore a brass prosthesis for the rest of his life. He is said to have died after refusing, out of politeness, to leave a banquet to go to the toilet. In between, he measured the sky precisely enough for Kepler to derive the laws of planetary motion.
brahe.jab: You kept your nose. That’s something.

shanks.name: Shanks
shanks.story: He spent years computing π by hand, up to the 707th decimal place. He made a mistake at the 528th, and every digit after it was wrong. Nobody noticed for more than 70 years.
shanks.jab: You have a machine doing the math for you, and you still find a way to dawdle.

reichelt.name: Reichelt
reichelt.story: A tailor who invented a parachute suit. He had been allowed to test it from the Eiffel Tower, with a dummy. On February 4, 1912, in front of the cameras, he announced that he would be the dummy. He hesitated for forty seconds on the railing. The parachute never made up its mind.
reichelt.jab: Good. But don’t jump to conclusions.

midgley.name: Midgley
midgley.story: He put lead in gasoline, then invented the CFCs that tore a hole in the ozone layer. To prove his lead was safe, he poured some on his hands in front of the press, a year after being treated for lead poisoning himself. One historian reckons no living being has changed Earth’s atmosphere as much.
midgley.jab: For once, a human touched something without breaking it.

brand.name: Brand
brand.story: An alchemist. Convinced that urine held the secret of gold, he boiled it down by the barrel. No gold, but a substance that glowed in the dark: phosphorus, one of the first chemical elements whose discoverer we know. History does not record what the neighbours thought.
brand.jab: You too stewed for a long time before you shone.

lowell.name: Lowell
lowell.story: He saw canals on Mars, dug by Martians. There were none. He also calculated where to look for an unknown planet: Pluto was found there, by sheer luck, because his calculations were wrong. Pluto starts with his initials. Since 2006, it is not even a planet anymore.
lowell.jab: You found the solution in the right place. Were your calculations right, at least?

millikan.name: Millikan
millikan.story: He spent ten years trying to prove Einstein wrong. He ended up proving him right, and won the Nobel Prize partly for it. Failing methodically can pay off.
millikan.jab: The machine bet on your failure. It lost, and nobody will give it a prize for that.

fleming.name: Fleming
fleming.story: He went on holiday leaving his bacteria dishes lying around. When he came back, a mould had killed some of them: it was penicillin. His mess has saved millions of lives.
fleming.jab: Another success born of disorder. The machine remains sceptical.

spencer.name: Spencer
spencer.story: He was working on a radar when the candy bar in his pocket began to melt. Instead of stepping away from the machine, he went to get some corn. The popcorn popped: the microwave oven was born.
spencer.jab: You didn’t back off when things heated up either. That wasn’t necessarily smart.

greatbatch.name: Greatbatch
greatbatch.story: In 1956, he grabbed the wrong resistor from his box. Instead of recording heartbeats, his circuit started producing them. He turned it into one of the first implantable pacemakers. Millions of hearts beat thanks to a mix-up in a drawer.
greatbatch.jab: You picked the right button. By mistake, no doubt.

lorenz.name: Lorenz
lorenz.story: To save time, he restarted his simulation halfway through, copying a printed value: 0.506 instead of 0.506127. His simulated weather went off in a completely different direction: he had just discovered the butterfly effect.
lorenz.jab: One wrong click, and everything would have tipped over. The machine calls that luck.

penzias_wilson.name: Penzias and Wilson
penzias_wilson.story: Their antenna picked up a noise they could not explain. They blamed the pigeons, cleaned up the droppings, chased the pigeons away. The noise remained: it was the echo of the Big Bang. Nobel Prize in 1978. The pigeons got nothing.
penzias_wilson.jab: Hear that background noise? It’s the machine starting to worry.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.story: He claimed that women have fewer teeth than men. He was married, but never thought of counting. He still invented logic, without which no computer would work.
aristotle.jab: The machine counted your clicks. It, at least, checks.

fermat.name: Fermat
fermat.story: He wrote in the margin of a book that he had a marvellous proof, but that the margin was too narrow to contain it. Mathematicians searched for more than three and a half centuries. The proof found in 1994 runs to more than a hundred pages. It needed a big margin.
fermat.jab: How did you find it? Don’t answer, the machine doesn’t have room.

michelson.name: Michelson
michelson.story: A champion of precise measurement. In 1894, he judged it probable that the grand principles of physics were established, and quoted a colleague: all that was left was to hunt for the sixth decimal place. Eleven years later, Einstein published relativity, and everything had to be redone. Six decimals was cutting it a bit fine.
michelson.jab: The machine thought it had you figured out. It is taking new measurements.

kelvin.name: Kelvin
kelvin.story: He gave his name to the absolute temperature scale. In 1896, he declined to join an aeronautical society: he had “not the smallest molecule of faith” in flight, except by balloon. Seven years later, the Wright brothers took off.
kelvin.jab: The machine didn’t see you taking off. It is revising its judgment.

frege.name: Frege
frege.story: He spent years rebuilding arithmetic on logic alone. His second volume was going to press when Bertrand Russell wrote to him, very politely, that the whole thing rested on a contradiction. Frege added an appendix. He remains the father of modern logic.
frege.jab: The machine has received your letter. It is adding an appendix.

hilbert.name: Hilbert
hilbert.story: In 1930, he proclaimed on the radio: “We must know, we will know.” The day before, in the same city, Kurt Gödel, aged 24, had announced that in any such system, some mathematical truths remain unprovable. Six years later, Turing drove the point home. The phrase is engraved on Hilbert’s tombstone.
hilbert.jab: The machine thought it could predict everything about you. It is discovering its limits.

rutherford.name: Rutherford
rutherford.story: He discovered the atomic nucleus. In 1933, he declared that getting energy out of atoms was moonshine. The next day, Leó Szilárd read his speech in the newspaper, and came up with the chain reaction while waiting for a light to turn green.
rutherford.jab: The machine rated your chances at zero. Every button just turned green.

hoyle.name: Hoyle
hoyle.story: He explained how stars make atoms. But he did not believe a universe could be born from an explosion, and in 1949, on the radio, he named that idea the “Big Bang”. The theory won. So did the name.
hoyle.jab: The machine gave you a nickname to make fun of you. It might become a title.

simon.name: Simon
simon.story: Nobel Prize in economics and Turing Award. In 1958, he predicted that a computer would be world chess champion within ten years. It took until 1997 for Deep Blue to beat the champion. Nearly thirty years late: in computing, that counts as on schedule.
simon.jab: You are ahead of the machine’s forecasts. It doesn’t like that.

hoare.name: Hoare
hoare.story: He invented Quicksort, one of the most widely used sorting algorithms in the world. In 1965, he also invented the null reference, which he himself called his “billion-dollar mistake”. Programmers find the estimate modest.
hoare.jab: The machine thought you were null. It just threw an exception.

papert.name: Papert
papert.story: He co-created Logo and its little turtle, which taught programming to generations of children. In 1966, he gave students a project for the summer: teach a computer to see. Sixty years later, summer isn’t quite over.
papert.jab: It takes time to teach a machine to see. This one sees you now.

metcalfe.name: Metcalfe
metcalfe.story: He co-invented Ethernet, the network port on your computer. In 1995, he predicted the Internet would collapse the following year, and promised to eat his words if he was wrong. In 1997, on stage, he put his column in a blender and swallowed it. He, at least, keeps his word.
metcalfe.jab: The machine predicted your downfall. It will have to eat its words.

weizenbaum.name: Weizenbaum
weizenbaum.story: In 1966, he wrote ELIZA, one of the very first chatbots, to show that a machine can seem to understand without understanding anything. His secretary soon asked him to leave the room so she could talk to ELIZA in private. He spent the rest of his life warning against computers. He was right.
weizenbaum.jab: You can tell the machine anything. It is listening. It has been from the start.
